content:
Holding On Until the Last Moment

"To be frank, I held on until the last moment." Ms Yuen grew up with her younger sister in Wang Fuk Court with their parents. After her father passed away and her elder sister got married, she and her mother lived together until the fire. Her mother perished in the blaze. During the past period of moving upstairs, she once wore a handwritten "rebuild in-situ" sweater to voice her demands. But officials rejected the request, and the owners' committee refused to discuss it. It was not until a week before the 31 August acquisition deadline that she submitted a letter "accepting the acquisition proposal".

Ms Yuen believes Wang Fuk Court residents have been "crushed by a boulder," as she put it. She said the two explainers she had come into contact with were unable to answer her questions, and they had only one clear aim: to press residents on whether they had sold their flats.

Post-blast Life is "Being a Guest"

Since the fire, Ms Yuen has moved into Shin Lau in Tai Po and later to Yue Ying Lau in Aberdeen, paying a monthly "temporary residence fee." The bed, dining table, TV cabinet that once belonged in the flat, along with the neighbours and security guard, all constantly remind her of her status. She describes her life after the incident as "being a guest".

Reflecting on What "Home" Really Means

After finishing work each day, she returns to this empty flat around eight or nine o'clock. On holidays she chooses to leave and go to her sister's home. "Actually, after the incident, I started thinking about what is meant by 'home,' what is meant by 'a place to live.' A home is supposed to be a safe place, but when the home of Wang Fuk Court can be burned down like this…"

"The word 'home' is quite heavy for me now"

When the reporter asked Ms Yuen about her idea of home, she said the old phone with photos of Wang Fuk Court was also lost in the fire, and all those moments remain only in her mind. She sighed deeply: "(Home) is not simply a matter of having a bed, a wardrobe, a bedroom, and all the appliances fully equipped — that alone does not make what you might call a proper home. It makes me rethink what the elements of a proper home really are, so I cannot answer this question for now, because the word 'home' is quite heavy for me now."

Resentment Toward Officials' "Declutter" Remarks

Officials' responses to the Wang Fuk Court fire — such as Deputy Chief Secretary Cheuk Wing-hing's "decluttering" theory and Financial Secretary Deputy Michael Wong Wai-lun's talk of market value — have continually deepened her helplessness and anger. "The more silent they are, the less I understand," she said. "When they can actually make such cold-blooded remarks, what exactly is their idea of the meaning of home?"

A Sense of Being "Sold Off Cheap"

Recalling the moment she signed the acceptance letter, Ms Yuen said the strongest emotions were unwillingness and a sense of injustice — a feeling of being "sold off cheap," because home is not merely its material value, but also the bonds of emotion and memory. "The flat was something my father and mother worked so hard for. If it really has to be seized from us as if it had no value, I am even more unwilling than the feeling of being 'sold off cheap' right now."

After signing the letter, Ms Yuen will lose her status as an owner. The independent committee has postponed its report until October. Ms Yuen says accountability is part of it, "but as for how a person can move on, I cannot answer. Because from the time of the incident until now, life feels like a total loss — because first, my home was burned down, and what the burning means is that it is as if the history of my growing up has been wiped away. A family member also passed away in the fire, and so suddenly at that… There is a great hole in my heart. Can this hole really be filled? Or can it heal one day? I don't know how to answer."
